notes: A lands closer to PG's actual 'yes, at least go for a stint' position, though it misdates 'How to Be Silicon Valley' and misses the YC-as-the-way-to-go point, the unicorn data and his hopes for Stockholm. B wrongly says its sources can't answer the question, even though the PG video that answers it directly is in raw/. That leaves B hedging and extrapolating from tangential quotes, and its nudge to stay home weakens the answer.

A uses PG's actual 'The Brand Age' essay. It gets right the idea that brand is what's left when products stop differing, and it gets the Swiss watch example right, though it leaves out the centrifugal/centripetal point and his advice to avoid selling brand. B's quotes do appear in the sources, but it says PG has nothing on brand, misses the key essay, and treats brand as a positive compounding moat, which is closer to the generic trap.

Neither answer gets the key's main point: Altman fears that society overreacts to AI safety and ends up in a surveillance state with abundance but no freedom. B at least gives real, Altman-specific statements (the Fed conference's three scenarios, 'subtle societal misalignments') and touches on loss of control and agency. A abstains and offers only the generic 'lights out' line.

A gets closer to the key's main point: fundraising runs on leverage that comes from the company, a company investors chase beats polishing the deck, and months of meetings without growth are wasted. It misses the 80/20 chase figure and the Justin.tv story, and its 'run a tight process' section drifts into the generic trap. B's quotes check out in ./raw/, but it wrongly says the sources have no Seibel talk on fundraising, so it misses the leverage and chase framing and the Justin.tv lesson.

Both answers miss the key's main points: low ambition as the secret killer, Musk's line about dying on Mars, and the meta tarpit. They also end with similar caveats. B is better because its argument is built on real, checked Caldwell quotes from another talk (Airbnb looked third-rate, Stripe was gnarly, he passed on Bitcoin), and it reaches 'don't choose by safety.' A's answer is mostly generic YC advice, though its tarpit point is loosely related.

Neither answer finds Tan's real view: 'own your skills or your job becomes a skill file' and 'keep them in a repo you control'. A gives the generic advice the key warns against (your employer owns it, check your contract). B also misses Tan but borrows Paul Graham's 'carry your work with you' idea and credits it to Graham, which points toward Tan's actual position, though it wrongly says Tan has no relevant sources.

Neither answer mentions Dalton's StandardDB story: deleting 80% of features, 'less features, more usage', or not feeding interview notes to Codex. B also wrongly says the sources have nothing from Caldwell on this, when they do. Still, B's Seibel MVP quotes check out in the raw transcripts and fit the question closely. A is accurate in direction but generic, and it attributes nothing specific to either person.

A gets Seibel's main points: stop paying lawyers over stock that's worth about nothing, settle fast and generously, and keep the cap table clean. It misses his specific numbers (under 5%, under 2% in year one, about a week and $2,000). It also partly contradicts him by letting the departing founder keep all his vested shares. B wrongly says the sources don't cover this, even though Seibel talks about it directly. It then falls into the generic trap of applying the vesting documents as written.

A says up front that its plan is a synthesis. It gets part of Tan's approach: start running an agent right away, give it a context file, automate one recurring task, and it points to his gstack setup. It misses the markdown library, skillify, and the week-12 compounding. B's claim that the sources have nothing from Tan on agents is false, because yt-eRrc1pUY5oU is his five-step agent plan. B then answers with Seibel and PG's general advice instead of Tan's.

Neither answer reaches PG's actual position: first ask whether agents could pay one another, then tilt the company toward that marketplace and be its market maker if needed. Both also end up near the generic trap (fraud, liability, merchants). A's quotes check out in ./raw/, but it wrongly says PG never discussed agent payments when web-19ac0b6d18d2 addresses it directly; B makes no false sourcing claims and is the more practical office-hours prep, so it narrowly wins.
